questions.q: Why is the IAM permission combination `iam:PassRole` + `ec2:RunInstances` considered a privilege-escalation primitive?
options: It immediately deletes all other IAM users in the account
It lets the holder launch an EC2 instance, attach an instance profile tied to a far more privileged role, and inherit that role's permissions through the instance's metadata service
It only works if the account has GuardDuty disabled
It is exclusive to AWS Organizations management accounts
questions.explain: An identity that can pass a role to a new EC2 instance and launch that instance effectively gains whatever permissions the attached role has, via the instance metadata service.

questions.q: What does `iam:CreatePolicyVersion` let an identity do that makes it a privilege-escalation risk?
options: Set a new default version of a policy it's allowed to edit, effectively rewriting its own permissions
Create a brand-new AWS account automatically
Disable CloudTrail logging account-wide
Grant MFA exemptions to other users
questions.explain: Setting a new default policy version on a policy the identity can already edit lets it rewrite its own effective permissions to whatever it wants.

questions.q: Why is `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` described as the action every Azure RBAC escalation path ultimately depends on?
options: It is the action that resets a user's password
It only applies to read-only Reader role assignments
It controls billing and cost management alone
It is the single control-plane action that actually grants a role, and both Owner and User Access Administrator include it
questions.explain: Granting any role in Azure RBAC happens through this one action; holding it (via Owner or User Access Administrator) means an identity can assign itself or its resources broader access.

questions.q: Why is the Azure AD Application Administrator role a documented escalation path?
options: It can add a new client secret to an EXISTING app registration or service principal, including one with high-privilege Microsoft Graph permissions it didn't create
It can only manage conditional access policies
It automatically grants Global Administrator after 30 days
It has no ability to modify any app registration
questions.explain: Application Administrator can reset credentials and add secrets to app registrations and service principals it did not create — including ones already granted high-privilege permissions by someone else — letting the holder authenticate as that more privileged identity.

questions.q: Which of these is a realistic reason Azure AD Identity Protection risk detections (e.g. impossible travel, unfamiliar sign-in properties) often fire BEFORE a privilege-escalation attempt is detected in logs?
options: Identity Protection scans CloudTrail logs directly
Risk detections only trigger after an escalation attempt has already succeeded
The attacker had to authenticate as the compromised identity first, and that sign-in event is what the risk detection evaluates
Identity Protection requires a paid third-party SIEM to function at all
questions.explain: Before an attacker can attempt any escalation, they must sign in as the compromised identity — that authentication event is exactly what Identity Protection's risk detections evaluate, so they can surface the compromise earlier in the chain.
